sources.citation: Simons, D. J., & Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception, 28(9), 1059–1074.
sources.notes: Primary Harvard study (N=192 across 16 main conditions + N=12 in the 9-second chest-thumping gorilla condition). Reports 46% overall inattentional blindness, 50% blindness for the 9s chest-thumping gorilla, 27% vs 58% noticing for White vs Black team attendance, and 64% vs 45% noticing for Easy vs Hard counting.

sources.citation: Neisser, U., & Becklen, R. (1975). Selective looking: Attending to visually specified events. Cognitive Psychology, 7(4), 480–494.
sources.notes: Foundational selective-looking paradigm using superimposed basketball passing and hand-slapping games that inspired Simons & Chabris (1999).

sources.citation: Memmert, D. (2006). The effects of eye movements, age, and expertise on inattentional blindness. Consciousness and Cognition, 15(3), 620–627.
sources.notes: Eye-tracking study on the Simons & Chabris gorilla video proving that observers who missed the gorilla fixated directly on it for an average of ~1 second, identical to observers who noticed it.

sources.citation: Drew, T., Võ, M. L.-H., & Wolfe, J. M. (2013). The Invisible Gorilla strikes again: Sustained inattentional blindness in expert observers. Psychological Science, 24(9), 1848–1853.
sources.notes: 20 of 24 (83%) expert radiologists searching lung CT scans for nodules missed a gorilla 48 times the size of an average nodule despite looking directly at its location on eye-tracking.

sources.citation: Simons, D. J. (2010). Monkeying around with the gorillas in our midst: Familiarity with an inattentional-blindness task does not improve the detection of unexpected events. i-Perception, 1(1), 3–6.
sources.notes: The 'Monkey Business Illusion' follow-up: viewers familiar with the gorilla spotted it, but missed the background curtain changing from red to gold and a black-team player walking off.

sources.citation: Bredemeier, K., & Simons, D. J. (2012). Working memory and inattentional blindness. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 19(2), 239–244.
sources.notes: Refutes the misconception that individual differences in working memory capacity predict who notices unexpected objects in sustained inattentional blindness.

sources.citation: Simons, D. J., & Jensen, M. S. (2009). The effects of individual differences and task difficulty on inattentional blindness. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 16(2), 398–403.
sources.notes: Shows that while harder primary counting tasks increase blindness, an individual's skill at the counting task does not predict noticing.

sources.citation: Chabris, C. F., Weinberger, A., Fontaine, M., & Simons, D. J. (2011). You do not talk about Fight Club if you do not notice Fight Club: Inattentional blindness for a simulated real-world assault. i-Perception, 2(2), 150–153.
sources.notes: Real-world replication inspired by Boston police officer Kenny Conley: volunteers jogging after a confederate missed a staged 3-person fight 65% of the time at night (35% noticed) and 44% during the day (56% noticed).

sources.citation: Most, S. B., Simons, D. J., Scholl, B. J., Jimenez, R., Clifford, E., & Chabris, C. F. (1999/2001). How not to be seen: The contribution of similarity and selective ignoring to sustained inattentional blindness. Psychological Science, 12(1), 9–17.
sources.notes: Demonstrates attentional set and selective ignoring: even a bright red cross moving across a black-and-white display for 5 seconds was missed by ~30% of observers.

sources.citation: Strayer, D. L., Drews, F. A., & Johnston, W. A. (2003). Cell phone-induced failures of visual attention during simulated driving. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 9(1), 23–32.
sources.notes: Eye-tracking in driving simulators showed hands-free phone conversations cause inattentional blindness even for objects directly fixated on the road.

sources.citation: Hyman, I. E., Boss, S. M., Wise, B. M., McKenzie, K. E., & Caggiano, J. M. (2010). Did you see the unicycling clown? Inattentional blindness while walking and talking on a cell phone. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 24(5), 597–607.
sources.notes: Pedestrians talking on cell phones walked right past a brightly dressed clown riding a unicycle across a campus square without noticing.

sources.citation: Rees, G., Russell, C., Frith, C. D., & Driver, J. (1999). Inattentional blindness versus inattentional amnesia for fixated but ignored words. Science, 286(5449), 2504–2507.
sources.notes: fMRI study proving that when attention is consumed by a primary task, the brain fails to process the meaning of ignored stimuli even at the center of gaze.

sources.citation: Simons, D. J. (2000). Attentional capture and inattentional blindness. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 4(4), 147–155.
sources.notes: Comprehensive review of explicit vs implicit attentional capture and inattentional blindness across lab and real-world settings.

sources.citation: Simons, D. J., & Chabris, C. F. (1999). Selective Attention Test [Original 1999 experiment stimulus video]. VisCog Productions / Daniel Simons YouTube Archive.
sources.notes: Original 1999 Harvard William James Hall 9-second chest-thumping gorilla stimulus video (82s with instruction and answer cards; 15 White-team passes).
